statement: Grandma bakes some cookies. She gives half of them to Ana and a quarter of them to Ben. Ana gets 4 more cookies than Ben. How many cookies did Grandma bake?

choices.misconception: I found how many cookies Ben gets, not how many Grandma baked.
I thought the 4 extra cookies were half of all the cookies.
I found how many cookies Ana and Ben get together and thought that was all of them.
I found that Grandma baked 16 cookies and then added the 4 extra cookies again.

hints: How much bigger is a half than a quarter?
Draw a bar for all the cookies and split it into 4 equal parts. Ana gets 2 parts and Ben gets 1 part. The difference between their shares is a number of parts you can see.
Ana's 2 parts are 1 part more than Ben's 1 part. So 1 part, a quarter, is the 4 extra cookies.

solutions.reliable: Split the cookies into 4 equal parts. Ana gets half, which is 2 parts. Ben gets a quarter, which is 1 part. Ana has 1 part more, and that part is 4 cookies. So each part is 4 cookies, and all 4 parts are $4 \times 4 = 16$ cookies. Check: Ana gets 8, Ben gets 4, and 8 is 4 more than 4. The idea to keep: turn fractions into equal parts of a bar, then find what one part is worth.
solutions.elegant: Half take away a quarter is a quarter, so a quarter of the cookies is 4. The whole is four quarters: 16.

whyOnTest: Comparing two fractions of the same whole needs a picture of equal parts, and the trap answers stop at a part instead of the whole.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
